difficultyReason: Transparent correlation-to-causation flaw in a short, two-sentence stimulus. Only (C) replicates the exact move — an observed correlation treated as proof of causation. Other choices commit obviously different errors or are valid.
stimulus: Students who eat breakfast every day score higher on math tests than students who skip breakfast. Therefore, eating breakfast causes students to do better in math.
questionStem: Which one of the following exhibits flawed reasoning most similar to that in the argument above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Runners who wear expensive shoes tend to finish races faster than those who don't. So expensive shoes must be worth the money.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Every swan I have ever seen has been white. Therefore, all swans are white.

choices.label: C
choices.text: People who own dogs tend to live longer than people who do not. Therefore, owning a dog causes people to live longer.

choices.label: D
choices.text: If it rains, the grass will be wet. The grass is wet, so it must have rained.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The new drug worked for my neighbor. Therefore, it should be approved for everyone.

explanations.correct: Stimulus: observed correlation (breakfast-eaters score higher) is treated as proof that breakfast causes the higher scores. (C) replicates the exact move: correlation between dog ownership and longevity is treated as proof that owning a dog causes longer life.
explanations.A: Tempting because it sounds causal, but the conclusion is evaluative ('worth the money'), not a causal claim. Different structure.
explanations.B: Unwarranted generalization from a sample, not correlation-to-causation.
explanations.D: Affirms the consequent — a conditional flaw, not a causal one.
explanations.E: Generalization from a single case, not correlation-to-causation.

difficultyReason: Sufficient-necessary confusion stated plainly. Only (B) reverses a conditional in the same way. Other answers are valid or commit transparently different errors.
stimulus: If a plant receives sunlight, it will grow. The fern in my kitchen is growing. Therefore, it must be receiving sunlight.
questionStem: The flawed reasoning in which one of the following is most similar to the flawed reasoning in the argument above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: If a student studies hard, she will pass the exam. Dana studied hard, so Dana passed the exam.

choices.label: B
choices.text: If it snows, the schools close. The schools are closed today. Therefore, it must be snowing.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Most people who exercise feel healthier. Marcus exercises, so Marcus probably feels healthier.

choices.label: D
choices.text: All mammals have lungs. A whale is a mammal. Therefore, a whale has lungs.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The more you practice piano, the better you get. Elena practices every day, so she is improving.

explanations.correct: Stimulus form: 'If P then Q; Q; therefore P' — affirming the consequent, a sufficient-necessary confusion. (B) runs the identical move: 'If snow then schools close; schools are closed; therefore snowing.'
explanations.A: Valid reasoning — if studying hard is sufficient, then a hard-studying student passes. No flaw.
explanations.C: No conditional reversal; a probabilistic inference applied straightforwardly.
explanations.E: No flaw — applying a stated pattern to a case.

difficultyReason: Unwarranted generalization from a tiny, unrepresentative sample. Only (D) replicates the same leap from a handful of cases to a sweeping claim.
stimulus: I've read three novels by contemporary British authors, and I disliked all three. Contemporary British fiction is clearly not worth reading.
questionStem: Which one of the following contains a pattern of flawed reasoning most similar to that in the argument above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The last two movies directed by Silva flopped at the box office. Therefore, Silva's next movie will also flop.

choices.label: B
choices.text: This restaurant serves excellent pasta. Therefore, it probably serves excellent risotto as well.

choices.label: C
choices.text: If a painting is by Goya, it is valuable. This painting is valuable, so it must be by Goya.

choices.label: D
choices.text: I've eaten at four Vietnamese restaurants in the city, and all four had slow service. Vietnamese restaurants in this city are just slow.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Jazz venues have been closing in our city. Therefore, live music in general is dying out.

explanations.correct: Stimulus: a few personal experiences (three novels) are used to condemn an entire category (contemporary British fiction). (D) does the same: four restaurant visits used to condemn every Vietnamese restaurant in the city.
explanations.A: Predicts a future event from a pattern — different structure (forecast, not sweeping generalization about a category).
explanations.B: Compositional extension from one dish to another — not a sample-to-population move.
explanations.C: Affirming the consequent — a conditional flaw, not generalization.
explanations.E: Scope shift from one subcategory (jazz) to a broader category (live music), not a small-sample generalization.

difficultyReason: Plain equivocation on a single word ('natural') across premise and conclusion. Only (A) shifts meaning of one term between premise and conclusion.
stimulus: Everything natural is good for you. Poison ivy grows naturally in the forest. Therefore, poison ivy is good for you.
questionStem: Which one of the following exhibits flawed reasoning most similar to that in the argument above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Nothing is better than eternal happiness. A cold sandwich is better than nothing. Therefore, a cold sandwich is better than eternal happiness.

choices.label: B
choices.text: All fruits are healthy. An apple is a fruit. Therefore, an apple is healthy.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Most athletes train daily. Priya is an athlete. Therefore, Priya probably trains daily.

choices.label: D
choices.text: If a law is unjust, it should not be obeyed. This law is unjust. Therefore, it should not be obeyed.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Exercise improves health. Marta exercises. Therefore, Marta is healthy.

explanations.correct: Stimulus: 'natural' shifts meaning from 'wholesome / good-for-you natural' (premise 1) to 'occurring in nature' (premise 2). (A) equivocates on 'nothing' — 'no thing is better' vs. 'is better than no food at all.' Same meaning-shift flaw.
explanations.B: Valid categorical syllogism — no equivocation, no flaw.
explanations.C: Valid probabilistic inference; no shift in meaning.
explanations.E: Overreaches from 'improves health' to 'is healthy,' but no single word shifts meaning — different flaw.

difficultyReason: Correlation-to-causation in an economics setting. Only (E) treats a co-occurring trend as proof of causation. Other answers are valid or commit clearly different errors.
stimulus: In countries where citizens drink more coffee, average life expectancy is higher. Drinking more coffee, therefore, must increase life expectancy.
questionStem: The flawed reasoning in which one of the following most closely parallels the flawed reasoning above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: If a country has a high GDP, it tends to have low unemployment. This country has low unemployment, so it must have a high GDP.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Two of my coworkers caught colds this week. Everyone at work is going to get sick.

choices.label: C
choices.text: All European nations use the euro. Germany is a European nation. Therefore, Germany uses the euro.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The stock market rose last year, and so did housing prices. The stock market rise must have caused the housing prices to climb.

choices.label: E
choices.text: A used car that looks clean is probably well-maintained. This car looks clean. So it's probably well-maintained.

explanations.correct: Stimulus: two things rise together (coffee consumption, life expectancy) and the author concludes one causes the other. (D) is the same move: stock market and housing prices both rose, so one caused the other.
explanations.A: Affirming the consequent — a conditional flaw, not correlation-to-causation.
explanations.B: Hasty generalization from two cases, not a causal leap from correlation.
explanations.C: Valid categorical reasoning. The premise is actually false, but the structure is not flawed.
explanations.E: Applies a general pattern to a specific case — no flaw, and not causal reasoning.

difficultyReason: Classic affirming-the-consequent in a legal context. Only (B) reverses a stated conditional. The other answers present valid reasoning or different fallacies.
stimulus: Any defendant who forged the signature had access to the notary's office. Ms. Lowe had access to the notary's office. Therefore, Ms. Lowe forged the signature.
questionStem: Which one of the following arguments exhibits flawed reasoning most similar to that in the argument above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Anyone who wins the marathon trains daily. Ravi did not train daily. Therefore, Ravi did not win the marathon.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Any hiker who reached the summit carried a rope. Dana carried a rope. Therefore, Dana reached the summit.

choices.label: C
choices.text: All licensed pilots have passed the medical exam. Kira is a licensed pilot. Therefore, Kira has passed the medical exam.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Most violinists in the orchestra studied abroad. Tomas is a violinist in the orchestra. Therefore, Tomas probably studied abroad.

choices.label: E
choices.text: If the window is open, the alarm will sound. The alarm is sounding, so the window is open — unless the sensor is broken.

explanations.correct: Stimulus: having access was necessary for forgery, not sufficient; treating it as sufficient commits sufficient-necessary confusion. (B) makes the same error: carrying a rope was necessary for reaching the summit, but the argument treats it as sufficient.
explanations.A: Valid — denying the necessary condition. No flaw.
explanations.D: Valid probabilistic inference from 'most' — no flaw.
explanations.E: Hedges the conclusion; the 'unless' clause avoids the flaw the stimulus commits.

difficultyReason: Unwarranted generalization in a technology context. Only (A) jumps from a single case to a sweeping verdict on a whole category. Other answers commit transparently different flaws.
stimulus: My new tablet froze twice in the first week. Clearly, tablets from this manufacturer are unreliable.
questionStem: Which one of the following contains a pattern of flawed reasoning most similar to that in the argument above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The first two chapters of this textbook contained errors. The whole textbook must be poorly edited.

choices.label: B
choices.text: If a phone battery is damaged, it drains quickly. This phone's battery drains quickly, so it must be damaged.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Most users of this software report bugs. Teo is a user, so he has probably reported a bug.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Apps that go viral usually have clever marketing. This app has clever marketing. Therefore, it will go viral.

choices.label: E
choices.text: New cars with high safety ratings sell well. This car has a high safety rating, so it will sell well — if people hear about it.

explanations.correct: Stimulus: a tiny experience (two freezes in one unit) is projected onto an entire manufacturer's product line. (A) mirrors the move: defects in two chapters are projected onto the whole textbook.
explanations.D: Sufficient-necessary confusion — treats marketing as sufficient when it's only typical.
explanations.E: Hedges the conclusion and therefore is not clearly flawed.

difficultyReason: Equivocation on the word 'right' across premise and conclusion in an ethics stimulus. Only (C) matches by shifting the meaning of a single term between premises.
stimulus: Every citizen has a right to free speech. Whatever a person has a right to do is the right thing to do. Therefore, whatever a citizen says is the right thing to say.
questionStem: Which one of the following exhibits flawed reasoning most similar to that in the argument above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: All triangles have three sides. This figure has three sides. Therefore, this figure is a triangle.

choices.label: B
choices.text: People who skip meals are often tired. Lin skips meals. So Lin is often tired.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A sound investment is a safe one. Soundproof walls keep noise out. Therefore, walls that keep noise out are safe investments.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Most voters prefer candidate Reyes. Maria is a voter. So Maria probably prefers Reyes.

choices.label: E
choices.text: When temperatures drop, ice forms. Ice has formed. So temperatures have dropped.

explanations.correct: Stimulus: 'right' shifts from 'entitled/permitted' to 'morally correct.' (C) equivocates on 'sound': 'safe/sensible investment' vs. 'sound as in noise.' Same single-word meaning shift across premises.
explanations.A: Valid structure except that having three sides is sufficient for being a triangle — no equivocation.
explanations.B: Valid probabilistic inference. No meaning shift.

difficultyReason: Correlation-to-causation in an environmental-policy setting. Only (B) treats co-occurrence as causation. Others commit different errors or reason validly.
stimulus: Cities that installed more bike lanes last decade saw air quality improve over the same period. Installing bike lanes, therefore, causes air quality to improve.
questionStem: Which one of the following contains a pattern of flawed reasoning most similar to that in the argument above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Recent graduates who attended networking events got jobs within six months. Attending networking events must make graduates more competent.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Neighborhoods that planted more street trees last year reported lower crime rates. Planting street trees must cause crime to drop.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Any runner who finishes the race gets a medal. Oskar got a medal, so Oskar must have finished the race.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Every play I've seen at this theater has been disappointing. The theater must never put on good plays.

choices.label: E
choices.text: A solar panel works when it receives light. This panel is working, so it must be receiving light.

explanations.correct: Stimulus: two trends co-occurred in the same places (more bike lanes, better air) and the author concludes causation. (B) is the same move: tree-planting and crime drops co-occurred, and the author infers causation.
explanations.A: Tempting, but the conclusion shifts topic to 'competence' rather than to getting jobs — scope shift rather than pure correlation-to-causation.
explanations.D: Unwarranted generalization from a sample, not correlation-to-causation.
explanations.E: Valid — requires light, has light, so it works. No flaw.

difficultyReason: Sufficient-necessary confusion in a linguistics context. Only (E) reverses a stated conditional. Others are valid or commit different fallacies.
stimulus: Anyone fluent in Portuguese can understand some written Spanish. Carla can understand some written Spanish. Therefore, Carla is fluent in Portuguese.
questionStem: The flawed reasoning in which one of the following is most similar to the flawed reasoning in the argument above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Every experienced translator knows at least two languages. Yuki is not an experienced translator. So Yuki doesn't know two languages.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Most native speakers of a language speak it without an accent. Sven is a native speaker, so Sven probably speaks without an accent.

choices.label: C
choices.text: People who read a lot have large vocabularies. Reading, therefore, causes vocabulary to grow.

choices.label: D
choices.text: My two roommates are studying German. Everyone in our building must be studying German.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Everyone who has taken the advanced class can recite the declensions. Nadia can recite the declensions. Therefore, Nadia has taken the advanced class.

explanations.correct: Stimulus: fluency in Portuguese is sufficient for understanding some written Spanish, but the argument treats it as necessary — classic sufficient-necessary reversal. (E) runs the same move: taking the advanced class is sufficient for reciting the declensions, but the argument treats it as necessary.
explanations.A: Denying a necessary condition — different structure (and valid, if one reads the conditional as stated).
explanations.B: Valid probabilistic inference from 'most.' No flaw.
